analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers wipe out private student loans in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on January 15, 2025, and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, almost no one can wipe out a student loan in bankruptcy unless they can prove repaying it would cause 'undue hardship' — a standard so strict that most people never qualify, and it applies even to loans from private companies. This bill would change the bankruptcy code so that loans from private lenders can be discharged like credit card debt or medical debt, while government-backed loans keep the stricter rule. The bill has been sitting in the House Judiciary Committee since it was introduced.
analysis.who_benefits: People carrying private student loan debt who file for bankruptcy. Today they must sue their lender inside bankruptcy and prove 'undue hardship,' a test courts interpret so strictly that most filers fail even when they are genuinely unable to pay. This bill would let them clear private loans the same way they clear other unsecured debts, giving a genuine fresh start to borrowers who took out high-interest loans from private companies rather than federal loans.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deletes the bankruptcy code's special protection for private education loans, so those loans can be discharged in bankruptcy without proving undue hardship [S3].
The change applies only to bankruptcy cases filed after the bill becomes law, and leaves the stricter hardship rule in place for government-backed loans [S3].
The Congressional Research Service confirms the bill 'allows private student loans to be discharged in bankruptcy regardless of whether a debtor demonstrates undue hardship' [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders and the investors who buy their loans. They would lose the ability to pursue borrowers indefinitely through the courts, and would recover nothing from borrowers who discharge their loans in bankruptcy. Some lenders would likely raise rates or tighten underwriting on future private loans to make up for the added risk, which would fall on future student borrowers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student loan lenders and investors

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is cost-shifting: lenders facing bankruptcy losses may charge higher interest rates or lend less to students without creditworthy cosigners, so the relief for distressed borrowers would partly be paid for by future borrowers in the form of pricier or scarcer private loans (a standard lender argument; not addressed in the provided sources).
The bill does nothing for the far larger group of borrowers with federal student loans, who would remain subject to the undue hardship test [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers already drowning in private loan debt, the bill offers real, targeted relief at a moment when bankruptcy is the only exit available. The costs — higher rates on future private loans and lost recoveries for lenders — are real but speculative in size, and the bill deliberately leaves federal loans untouched, limiting its reach. On balance it is a narrow, borrower-friendly fix rather than a sweeping debt-forgiveness program.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee on January 15, 2025, and the committee has taken no further action on it; nothing has been scheduled, so the bill is sitting, not dead.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill in the House on January 15, 2025 [S1].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, the only action recorded in its history [S5].
Five Democratic members joined as cosponsors: Reps. Danny Davis of Illinois, Eric Swalwell, Gwen Moore of Wisconsin, and Julia Brownley [S4].

Under the bill, private student loans — the category added to the bankruptcy code's exceptions in 2005 — would be dischargeable like credit card or medical debt, while government-backed loans keep the undue-hardship rule [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders benefit so far: the rule that makes their loans nearly impossible to escape in bankruptcy remains untouched, because the bill has not moved past referral.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 5 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on introduction (Reps. Davis of Illinois, Swalwell, Moore of Wisconsin, and Brownley).

for.name: Private student loan lenders and industry groups
for.what_they_did: Have long opposed letting private student loans be discharged in bankruptcy; no lobbying on this specific bill appears in the record.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor action on the bill since its referral on January 15, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on; the bill has not reached a vote, so its partisan split is only visible in the sponsor list so far.

industries.note: Private lenders hold the loans this bill would make dischargeable; today that non-dischargeable status lets them pursue delinquent borrowers for decades with wage garnishment and lawsuits. The industry's interest in keeping the current rule runs directly against borrowers' interest in a fresh start.

industries.industry: Student loan borrowers with federal loans
industries.note: The bill leaves federal loans under the undue-hardship rule, so federal borrowers get no direct relief — but by narrowing the exception to government-backed debt, it treats federal loans as the special protected category, which is where the political fight over student debt relief is centered.

analysis.trajectory: A bill sitting in the House Judiciary Committee with six Democratic supporters and no Republican cosponsors, with no hearing or markup scheduled, has a very long path to law: committee action, floor passage in a chamber Republicans control, and Senate action would all be needed. Versions of this proposal have been reintroduced across several Congresses without reaching a floor vote. Realistically, it will likely remain in committee unless there is a major shift in priorities or the composition of Congress.
